title: [chore]: Create AI Usage policy
body:
### Requirement

We need to have a stated policy about AI-assisted contributions, in particular some guardrails to prevent a flood of low quality PRs.

Relevant links:
  * https://github.com/grafana/tempo/pull/6127#issuecomment-3730110700

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: hey @reporter i could draft a policy for this purpose if needed

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant1 give it a try. I strongly recommend looking at other CNCF projects first that already have AI policies (and I disagree with some of them).

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
@reporter i checked out a few other policies, the major ones being Linux foundation's usage policy (https://<redacted-host>/legal/generative-ai), Kiali's policy (https://github.com/kiali/kiali/blob/master/AI_POLICY.md), and this linked discussion - https://github.com/cncf/toc/issues/1803, as well OTel's policy (https://github.com/open-telemetry/community/blob/main/policies/genai.md)

Overall, I'm thinking of defining guidelines separated by what type of contributions are allowed (slight modifications, documentation assistance) vs. which aren't (blind submissions, 'vibe coding'), along with certain required practices. Will update with the exact policy.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Hey @reporter, have gone through the K8s policy thread you shared. 
Before writing policy text, I think it helps to agree on what we’re trying to prevent. The main goals seem to be author accountability like AI use is allowed, but the PR author must own the changes, understands them, tests them, and can explain them. Review shouldn’t be the first validation step. Other important goal can be transparency i.e simple disclosure of AI usage so reviewers aren’t guessing how the change was produced.

comments.author: participant3
comments.body: Avoiding large, unreviewable AI-generated diffs that increase maintainer burden and keeping review discussions human (no AI-generated review replies) can be some milestones

comments.author: reporter
participant2
comments.body:
Hey @reporter 
Thanks for the feedback – it makes sense to define the goals first before jumping into policy text.

Based on the K8s thread you linked and the discussion here, I think the main goals for Jaeger’s AI policy are:

**What we're trying to prevent**
1. Low‑quality PRs where the author doesn’t really understand the code they submitted
2. Large or mostly AI‑generated diffs that are hard to review and put extra burden on maintainers
3. AI‑generated review replies – reviewers want to discuss changes with the human author
4. Situations where contributors cannot explain or defend their changes during review

**What we want to enable**
1. Legitimate use of AI tools to improve productivity (docs, tests, small refactors, boilerplate)
2. Clear expectations so contributors know how they’re allowed to use AI in PRs
3. Clear grounds for maintainers to push back on problematic AI‑assisted PRs (e.g., huge unreviewable diffs or authors who can’t explain changes)

Does this capture what you had in mind? I’m happy to adjust these goals based on your feedback before I update the policy text in the PR.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
> Legitimate use of AI tools to improve productivity (docs, tests, small refactors, boilerplate)

I don't want to limit AI tools like this. There is nothing wrong with using AI for complex refactoring / rewrites / implementations. It's not about the complexity of the task, it's about the effort imbalance. Before AI the effort for a merged PR was split about 75:25 towards the contributor. With reckless use of AI this ratio skews 5:95 towards maintainer.

And the guidance to small PRs is a consistent guideline regardless of how it's produced, so it doesn't need to be in the AI policy.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: I was also recently considering how we can strengthen the CI system so that it can weed out PRs that do not pass CI conditions. The problem is that GH does not automatically run CI for new contributors. We can still have a workflow running off the main branch (which is safe and GH does not block those), but we cannot run unknown code there, so one possibility is introducing a flavor of "sign your commits" requirement where the last commit in the PR branch must contain verifiable evidence of tests that have been run locally. This could be a `make` target and runs the tests and amends the HEAD commit with a trailer.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hey @reporter 👋

Thanks for explaining – now I get it. The problem isn't about what AI does (small vs big tasks). It's about **who does the work**.

Before AI: contributor does 75% of the work, maintainer does 25%.
With careless AI use: contributor does 5%, maintainer gets stuck with 95%.

That's not fair to maintainers.

I also understand why checkboxes don't work – they're just one-time clicks that don't prove anything.

---

**Your CI idea got me thinking.** I did some research and here's one way we could make it work:

### Step 1: Add a `make verify` command

This would:
1. Run the tests locally (`make test`)
2. If tests pass, add a line to the commit message like:
This is called a "trailer" – same idea as `Signed-off-by` that Jaeger already uses for DCO.

Here's roughly how it could look in the Makefile:
```makefile
.PHONY: verify
verify: test
	@participant5 "✅ Tests passed. Adding trailer..."
	@participant6 commit --amend -m "$(git log -1 --pretty=%B)\n\nTested-By: $(git config user.name) <$(git config user.email)>"
```

### Step 2: Add a GitHub Action to check for the trailer

This would be a simple workflow that fails if my last commit doesn't have `Tested-By:`:
```yaml
name: Verify PR
on: pull_request

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Check for Tested-By trailer
        run: |
          if ! git log -1 --pretty=%B | grep -q "Tested-By:"; then
            echo "❌ Missing Tested-By trailer. Please run 'make verify' first."
            exit 1
          fi
```

### Step 3: Require this check before merging

You could add a branch protection rule so no PR can merge unless this check passes.

---

**Why I think this helps:**
- I (the contributor) have to actually run tests on my machine – not just tick a box
- My commit history shows real proof that I did the work
- It works even for new contributors like me, where CI might not run automatically
- You (the maintainer) can trust that I did the basic checks before asking for your time

---

**For the AI policy itself**, I'll keep it really short – focused on:
1. **Effort stays balanced** – I do the work, not you
2. **Real proof** – testing happens, not just promises
3. **Human conversations** – I reply to reviews myself, not AI

---

Does this direction make sense to you? If you think it's worth exploring, I'm happy to put together a small PR with:
- A short AI policy document
- The `make verify` target
- The GitHub Action to check for it

Just let me know what you think! 🙌

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
yep, sounds good. 

```
verify: lint test
```
Include the lint step.

> `@participant6 commit --amend -m "$(participant6 log -1 --pretty=%B)\n\nTested-By: $(participant6 config user.name) <$(participant6 config user.email)>"`

This is very easy to spoof, and AI is known for taking easy path, e.g. if a contributor points AI to CI results and asks "why did it fail" then the AI can simply find this instruction and run it itself. I would prefer something stronger. One alternative could be using `gh` cli to post test logs to a gist and attach the URL to the commit trailer. The validation could load the gist and check that it is for the right commit hash. This is harder to spoof and likely not worth spoofing.

> Add a GitHub Action to check for the trailer

The validation GH action should also be smarter. If a contributor is already established and the CI will run tests for their PR automatically there is no need to require manual proof of test.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
Hey @reporter 👋

You're right – the basic `Tested-By:` trailer is too easy to fake. An AI could just copy that line without actually running anything. I hadn't thought about that.

Your idea of uploading test logs to a Gist is much better. Here's how I think it could work:

---

### How `make verify` would work

When I run `make verify` before pushing my PR:

1. It runs lint (to catch basic code issues)
2. It runs tests
3. If both pass, it saves the test output to a file
4. It uploads that file to a Gist using `gh` CLI
5. It adds two lines to my commit message:
   - `Tested-By: Phani <<email-scrubbed>>` – shows who ran the tests
   - `Test-Gist: https://gist.github.com/...` – link to the actual test logs

Here's roughly how it would look:
```makefile
.PHONY: verify
verify: lint test
	@participant5 "✅ Lint and tests passed. Uploading proof..."
	@participant8 test > test.log 2>&1
	@participant9=$$(participant6 log -1 --pretty=%H); \
	GIST_URL=$$(gh gist create test.log -d "Test logs for $$COMMIT" --public); \
	MSG=$$(participant6 log -1 --pretty=%B); \
	NAME=$$(participant6 config user.name); \
	EMAIL=$$(participant6 config user.email); \
	participant6 commit --amend -m "$${MSG}\n\nTested-By: $${NAME} <$${EMAIL}>\nTest-Gist: $$GIST_URL"
```

**Why this is harder to fake:**
- You need real test logs, not just a copied line
- The Gist must have the right commit hash
- It's easier to just run the tests than to fake all this

---

### Smarter check for different contributors

You also said established contributors don't need extra checks – CI already runs for them. That makes sense.

So the GitHub Action could work like this:

| Who | What we check | Why |
|-----|---------------|-----|
| Established contributors (internal PRs) | Just `Tested-By:` | CI already runs for them |
| New contributors (PRs from forks) | `Tested-By:` + `Test-Gist:` with right commit | Proves they actually ran tests |

Here's a rough idea:
```yaml
name: Verify PR

on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Is this PR from a fork?
        id: fork
        run: |
          if [ "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }}" != "${{ github.repository }}" ]; then
            participant5 "external=true" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          else
            participant5 "external=false" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          fi

      - name: Check for Tested-By (everyone)
        run: |
          if ! participant6 log -1 --pretty=%B | grep -q "Tested-By:"; then
            participant5 "❌ No Tested-By trailer. Run 'make verify' first."
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Check Gist for new contributors
        if: steps.fork.outputs.external == 'true'
        run: |
          MSG=$(participant6 log -1 --pretty=%B)
          GIST_URL=$(participant5 "$MSG" | grep "Test-Gist:" | awk '{print $2}')
          
          if [ -z "$GIST_URL" ]; then
            participant5 "❌ New contributors need a Test-Gist trailer."
            exit 1
          fi

          COMMIT=$(participant6 log -1 --pretty=%H)
          if ! curl -s "$GIST_URL" | grep -q "$COMMIT"; then
            participant5 "❌ Gist doesn't match this commit."
            exit 1
          fi

          participant5 "✅ Looks good!"
```

---

### For the AI policy

I'll keep it short and focused on three things:

1. **Work stays balanced** – I do the work, not you
2. **Real proof** – test logs in a Gist, not just a checkbox
3. **Human replies** – I answer review comments myself, not AI

---

Does this sound right to you? If yes, I can start working on a PR with:
- A short AI policy
- The `make verify` command
- The GitHub Action.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Sounds good. But I would start with just the high level policy without the explicit validation rules, and then in another PR we can extend it.

We can check for non-members via GH API https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/enums#commentauthorassociation

> on: pull_request:

This cannot be the trigger because with it the workflow simply won't run for new people, exactly the problem with the CI. We need to run on `pull_request_target`.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
@reporter 
 That makes things much clearer. I'll split this into two PRs like you suggested.

---

## PR 1 (Now): Just the AI Policy

I'll create a simple `AI_USAGE_POLICY.md` file with high-level rules. No Makefile or GitHub Action stuff yet.

Here's what I'm thinking for the policy:

**What's okay:**
- Using AI tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.) to help you understand code
- Using AI to write drafts of code, tests, or docs
- Using AI to explore ideas or try different approaches
- Saying "AI helped me write this" – totally fine

**What's not okay:**
- Copy-pasting AI output without reading or understanding it
- Submitting code that doesn't work or doesn't compile
- Submitting PRs without running tests first
- Using AI to reply to review comments (reviewers want to talk to you, not a bot)

**Your responsibility:**
- You own everything you submit – even if AI wrote it
- You must understand your code well enough to explain it
- You must run tests locally before opening a PR
- If AI wrote a big chunk of your PR, mention that in the description

**Maintainer rights:**
- Maintainers can close PRs that look like low-effort AI spam
- Maintainers can ask questions if your replies sound auto-generated

I'll keep this short and simple – no technical enforcement details yet.

---

## PR 2 (Later): Technical Enforcement

After the policy PR merges, I'll open another PR with the actual enforcement:

**1. `participant8 verify-with-proof` command**

When a contributor runs this before pushing:
- It runs lint (catches basic code issues)
- It runs tests
- If both pass, it saves the test output to a file
- It uploads that file to a Gist using `gh` CLI
- It adds two lines to the commit message:
  - `Tested-By: Name <participant7>`
  - `Test-Gist: https://gist.github.com/...`

This is harder to fake because you need real test logs with the right commit hash.

**2. GitHub Action using `pull_request_target`**

You're right that `pull_request` won't work for new contributors – GitHub doesn't run it automatically for forks. So I'll use `pull_request_target` instead.

From the docs: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows#pull_request_target

This runs in the context of the base repo, so it works even for PRs from forks.

**3. Use `author_association` to check who's trusted**

Thanks for pointing me to: https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/enums#commentauthorassociation

I can use this to treat different contributors differently:

| Who | Values | What we check |
|-----|--------|---------------|
| Trusted (members) | `OWNER`, `MEMBER`, `COLLABORATOR` | Just `Tested-By:` – CI already runs for them |
| New contributors | `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIMER`, `NONE` | `Tested-By:` + `Test-Gist:` with matching commit hash |

This way:
- Trusted contributors don't have extra friction
- New contributors must prove they actually ran tests
- It's harder to fake than a simple checkbox

**4. Branch protection**

Once everything is working, we can add branch protection on `main` to require these checks before merging.

---

## Summary

| PR | What's in it | When |
|----|--------------|------|
| PR 1 | AI policy document (high-level rules only) | I'll open this soon |
| PR 2 | Makefile target + GitHub Action + docs update | After PR 1 merges |

---

Does this plan sound good to you? I'll start working on PR 1 with just the policy.

comments.author: ghost
comments.body:
I think we can also add a mandatory step in contributing guidelines that: Review your own PRs and add inline comments on that PR (review those changes which you think are difficult to understand). If there is no explanatory comments on any PR, maintainers will not review that PR. There maybe exception like: a contributor already discussed a lot with the maintainers before raising a PR in the corresponding issue/slack.

Also, the comment should explain "why" not only "what". So that if a contributor uses AI to generate any complex code, making them to explain it in their own words via comments will prove that they actually understand what the code is doing.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: @participant10 I certainly like the "why" explanations but I prefer them to be left as code comments, which serve as long term documentation, rather than PR comments that are difficult to find afterwards.

comments.body: Hi, I think that self-declaration along with the usage of [Agent Trace Specification](https://agent-trace.dev/) or something similar could be helpful, not just in the reviewing process, but also in long term documentation, etc.
